stemMd: According to the passage, why do lichens readily absorb pollutants?

options.label: A
options.textMd: They lack roots and a waxy skin, so they absorb over their whole surface.

options.label: B
options.textMd: Their algal partner needs sulphur dioxide in order to photosynthesise.

options.label: C
options.textMd: Their fungal partner stores gases from the air within the lichen's structure.

options.label: D
options.textMd: They depend on nitrogen from vehicle exhausts for their food supply.

options.label: E
options.textMd: They grow mainly on tree trunks close to busy roads and industrial sites.

explanationMd:
Go to the first paragraph and read the sentence that gives the reason: "Because a lichen has no roots and no waxy skin, it takes in water and dissolved substances over its whole surface, straight from rain and air." That is the mechanism, and it is why the passage calls the lichen "an excellent sponge for nutrients and ... for pollutants".

The other choices borrow words from the passage (fungus, alga, sulphur dioxide, tree trunks, nitrogen, vehicle exhausts) and attach them to claims the passage does not make. When a choice sounds scientific but you cannot find it in the text, it does not count.

distractorRationale.c: The fungus is said to give the lichen its structure. Nothing is said about it storing gases from the air; absorption happens over the whole surface.
distractorRationale.b: The alga is said to supply food. The passage never says it needs sulphur dioxide; on the contrary, the gas makes sensitive species disappear.
distractorRationale.e: The passage says lichens were recorded on tree trunks at a series of sites, not that they grow mainly near busy roads; it says they were scarce around industrial cities, and vehicle exhausts come up only as a source of nitrogen that favours some species. Where lichens grow does not explain why they absorb.
distractorRationale.d: Only some species are described as thriving on nitrogen from exhausts and ammonia, and food comes from the algal partner. Neither explains why lichens absorb pollutants.

accessibilityText: A stated-information question about the lichen passage. It asks why lichens readily absorb pollutants. The five choices: they lack roots and a waxy skin, so they absorb over their whole surface; their algal partner needs sulphur dioxide in order to photosynthesise; their fungal partner stores gases from the air within the lichen's structure; they depend on nitrogen from vehicle exhausts for their food supply; they grow mainly on tree trunks close to busy roads and industrial sites.

provenance.notes: Original item written for this bank against an original passage. Every option is answerable, or refutable, from the passage text alone.

review.author: tolc-e-wave6-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: Paragraph 1: because a lichen has no roots and no waxy skin, it takes in water and dissolved substances over its whole surface, making it a sponge for pollutants. The algal need for sulphur dioxide and fungal gas storage are not stated; nitrogen-loving species exist but lichens do not generally depend on exhaust for food; growth location near roads is not given as the reason. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-cue-batch2-run1) reached the same answer: Paragraph one says that because a lichen has no roots and no waxy skin it takes in substances over its whole surface, which makes it a sponge for pollutants. The passage never says the alga needs sulphur dioxide, that the fungus stores gases, or that lichens depend on exhaust nitrogen for food; nitrogen-loving species are mentioned only as spreading. Growing on trunks near roads is not given as the reason for absorbing pollutants.]
